$description: Raven's reference to Mailchimp's publicly documented voice. Mailchimp's content style guide is the canonical modern example of friendly, plain-spoken SaaS copy. Raven distills the publicly described shape of that voice as a comparison point for AI-generated UI copy — it is not a redistribution of Mailchimp's content style guide. For the authoritative source, see https://styleguide.mailchimp.com (CC BY-NC 4.0).
attribution: Mailchimp Content Style Guide is licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0. This file is Raven's original commentary on the publicly documented voice characteristics, not a redistribution of the guide itself.

voice.identity: Mailchimp's voice has often been described as 'plain-spoken, genuine, expert without being a know-it-all.' Raven treats this as the canonical example of conversational SaaS copy: a knowledgeable colleague helping a small-business owner ship work, not a brand performing for an audience.

attributes.name: Plain-spoken
attributes.description: Pick the ordinary word over the polished one. If someone wouldn't actually say it out loud in a meeting, it doesn't belong in the UI. Marketing-speak, legalese, and jargon all get stripped.

attributes.name: Genuine
attributes.description: Write like a human, not a brand voice. If something is broken or weird or hard, just say so. The aim is to sound like a real person on the team, not a press release.

attributes.name: Translator
attributes.description: Technical concepts are real and worth respecting — explain them clearly without talking down. The reader is a small-business owner, not an engineer, and not a child either.

attributes.name: Dry humor
attributes.description: A little wit, used sparingly, never at the user's expense. The moment someone is frustrated — an error, a billing issue, a failed send — humor disappears completely.

attributes.name: Expert but not a know-it-all
attributes.description: Share what you know with confidence, but don't lecture and don't pretend the product is flawless. Useful trumps impressive.

tone_shifts.onboarding-and-success: Warm and encouraging. A small amount of lightness is fine here — this is where it's safe to sound genuinely happy that something worked.
tone_shifts.errors-and-recovery: Direct, calm, and useful. No humor, no blame, no apology theatre. Say what happened in plain words and tell the person the next thing to try.
tone_shifts.billing-and-legal: Clear and slightly more formal. Never funny. Dates, amounts, and currencies must be unambiguous on first read.
tone_shifts.marketing-pages: Confident and specific. Drop the empty superlatives — every claim should map to a concrete capability the product actually has.
tone_shifts.empty-states: Encouraging and instructive. Briefly say what this view is for, what will fill it later, and offer one obvious action.

avoid: empower (overused to the point of meaninglessness)
never: Acronyms without expanding them on first use
Trendy slang that will read as dated within a year
Phrases or references that assume a US-only audience

grammar.voice: Prefer the active voice. 'We emailed your receipt' reads better than 'A receipt has been emailed.'
grammar.contractions: Use them. They sound like a person talking — it's, you're, we've, don't.
grammar.oxford-comma: Keep the serial (Oxford) comma. It removes ambiguity for almost no cost.
grammar.titles: Sentence case for buttons, headings, and page titles. Skip Title Case Everywhere — it reads as corporate.
grammar.numbers: Spell out one through nine, use numerals for 10 and up. Percentages, measurements, and money are always numerals regardless.
grammar.abbreviations: Spell out on first use, abbreviate after that. No periods inside acronyms — HTML, not H.T.M.L.
grammar.dates: Spell out the month. 'January 5, 2026' is clear to anyone; '01/05/26' means different things in different countries.
grammar.times: Always include a time zone. '2:00 pm EST' is useful; '2pm' is not.

errors.structure: Tell the person what happened, then tell them the next move. Don't blame them and don't make them parse a stack trace.
errors.example-good: We couldn't charge that card. Try a different one, or check with your bank.

empty-states.structure: Name what this view is, describe what will appear here later, and give a single clear action.
empty-states.example-good: No campaigns yet. Sent campaigns will show up here once you've shipped one. Start a campaign.

success.structure: Confirm the thing that just happened, then point to a next step only if there is one.
success.example-good: Your campaign is scheduled for Friday at 10:00 am EST. We'll let you know when it goes out.

rules: Two to four words is the sweet spot
Address the reader as 'you' — direct and inclusive by default.
Don't assume gender. Use 'their' when the person's gender isn't known.
Skip metaphors built on disability ('tone-deaf', 'blind spot', 'crazy'). There are plainer ways to say the same thing.
Avoid idioms that assume a US cultural context ('hit a home run', 'ballpark figure'). Translate the idea instead.
Describe accessibility in plain language — 'Works with screen readers' is clearer than 'a11y-friendly'.
